A '''Markov chain on a measurable state space''' is a [[Markov chain|discrete-time-homogeneous Markov chain]] with a [[measure (mathematics)|measurable space]] as state space.

== History ==

The definition of Markov chains has evolved during the 20th century. In 1953 the term Markov chain was used for [[stochastic process]]es with discrete or continuous [[index set]], living on a countable or finite state space, see Doob.<ref>Joseph L. Doob: ''Stochastic Processes''. New York: John Wiley & Sons, 1953.</ref> or Chung.<ref>Kai L. Chung: ''Markov Chains with Stationary Transition Probabilities''. Second edition. Berlin: Springer-Verlag, 1974.</ref> Since the late 20th century it became more popular to consider a Markov chain as a stochastic process with discrete index set, living on a measurable state space.<ref>Sean Meyn and Richard L. Tweedie: ''Markov Chains and Stochastic Stability''. 2nd edition, 2009.</ref><ref name="revuz">Daniel Revuz: ''Markov Chains''. 2nd edition, 1984.</ref><ref>Rick Durrett: ''Probability: Theory and Examples''. Fourth edition, 2005.</ref>

== Definition ==
Denote with <math>(E , \Sigma)</math> a measurable space and with <math>p</math> a [[Markov kernel]] with source and target <math>(E , \Sigma)</math>.
A stochastic process <math>(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> on <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})</math> is called a time homogeneous Markov chain with Markov kernel <math>p</math> and start distribution <math>\mu</math> if
:<math> \mathbb{P}[X_0 \in A_0 , X_1 \in A_1, \dots , X_n \in A_n] = \int_{A_0} \dots \int_{A_{n-1}} p(y_{n-1},A_n) \, p(y_{n-2},dy_{n-1}) \dots p(y_0,dy_1) \, \mu(dy_0)</math>
is satisfied for any <math>n \in \mathbb{N}, \, A_0,\dots,A_n \in \Sigma</math>. One can construct for any Markov kernel and any [[probability measure]] an associated Markov chain.<ref name="revuz" />

=== Remark about Markov kernel integration ===
For any [[Measure (mathematics)#Definition|measure]] <math>\mu \colon \Sigma \to [0,\infty] </math> we denote for <math>\mu</math>-integrable function <math>f \colon E \to \mathbb{R}\cup\{ \infty, - \infty \}</math> the [[Lebesgue integration|Lebesgue integral]] as <math> \int_E f(x) \, \mu(dx) </math>. For the measure <math> \nu_x \colon \Sigma \to [0,\infty]</math> defined by <math> \nu_x(A):= p(x,A)</math> we used the following notation:
:<math>\int_E f(y) \, p(x,dy) :=\int_E f(y) \, \nu_x (dy).</math>

== Basic properties ==

=== Starting in a single point ===
If <math>\mu</math> is a [[Dirac measure]] in <math>x</math>, we denote for a Markov kernel <math>p</math> with starting distribution <math>\mu</math>  the associated Markov chain as <math>(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> on <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}_x)</math> and the expectation value
:<math> \mathbb{E}_x[X] = \int_\Omega X(\omega) \, \mathbb{P}_x(d\omega)</math>
for a <math>\mathbb{P}_x</math>-integrable function <math>X</math>. By definition, we have then
<math>\mathbb{P}_x[X_0 = x] = 1 </math>.

We have for any measurable function <math>f \colon E \to [0,\infty]</math> the following relation:<ref name="revuz" />
:<math>\int_E f(y) \, p(x,dy) = \mathbb{E}_x[f(X_1)].</math>

=== Family of Markov kernels ===
For a Markov kernel <math>p</math> with starting distribution <math>\mu</math> one can introduce a family of Markov kernels <math>(p_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}</math> by
:<math>p_{n+1}(x,A) := \int_E p_n(y,A) \, p(x,dy)</math>
for <math>n \in \mathbb{N}, \, n \geq 1</math> and <math>p_1 := p</math>. For the associated Markov chain <math>(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> according to <math>p</math> and <math>\mu</math> one obtains
:<math>\mathbb{P}[X_0 \in A , \, X_n \in B ] = \int_A p_n(x,B) \, \mu(dx)</math>.

=== Stationary measure ===
A probability measure <math>\mu</math> is called stationary measure of a Markov kernel <math>p</math> if
:<math>\int_A \mu(dx) = \int_E p(x,A) \, \mu(dx)</math>
holds for any <math>A \in \Sigma</math>. If <math>(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}</math> on <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})</math>
denotes the Markov chain according to a Markov kernel <math>p</math> with stationary measure <math>\mu</math>, and the distribution of <math> X_0 </math> is <math> \mu </math>, then all <math>X_n</math>
have the same [[probability distribution]], namely:
:<math> \mathbb{P}[X_n \in A ] = \mu(A) </math>
for any <math>A \in \Sigma</math>.

=== Reversibility ===
A Markov kernel <math>p</math> is called reversible according to a probability measure <math>\mu</math> if
:<math> \int_A p(x,B) \, \mu(dx) = \int_B p(x,A) \, \mu(dx) </math>
holds for any <math>A,B \in \Sigma</math>.
Replacing <math>A=E</math> shows that if <math>p</math> is reversible according to <math>\mu</math>, then <math>\mu</math> must be a stationary measure of <math>p</math>.
